project_requirements.title: What the call wants
project_requirements.question: What must the project address, develop and achieve?

cards.title: Central object
cards.question: What is the principal thing the project must develop?
cards.answer:
AI-based cybersecurity systems, tools and services that help national cyber authorities and critical-infrastructure operators detect, analyse and respond to threats.
The topic also covers the security of the AI itself: the AI tools must be cybersecure, robust and trustworthy, and comply with the AI Act (the EU law on artificial intelligence), intellectual property law and the GDPR (the EU data-protection law).
cards.sources: Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 11–14 · CYBERAI, Objectives; Scope

cards.title: Scope
cards.question: Which activities fall within the funding opportunity's scope?
cards.answer:
A project must include at least one activity from the call's list; the topic names no excluded activities.
Optional activities (at least one required):
- Continuous pattern and anomaly detection for emerging threats, including in ICT or Operational Technology (OT, the systems that control physical equipment such as substations) infrastructures using open technologies
- Creating cyber threat intelligence (CTI, structured information on attackers and their methods) from new detection capabilities
- Faster incident response through real-time network monitoring, alerts or automated responses
- Malware mitigation by analysing code behaviour, network traffic and files
- Vulnerability identification and management from multiple information sources
- Cybersecure tools that reduce risk where AI, IoT (internet-connected devices) and smart grids or other manufacturing chains meet
- Recovery from incidents through self-healing capacities
- Automated vulnerability scanning and penetration testing
- Protecting business-sensitive data by detecting abnormal access patterns
- Sharing CTI without compromising privacy, through anonymisation
- Security by design in line with the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA, the EU law on security of products with digital elements)
- Tools to protect and secure AI solutions, and contributions to cybersecurity certification of AI-driven solutions
Tool and service providers are welcome, also in consortium with Cyber Hubs (national or cross-border centres that pool threat detection). The tools developed must be made available for licensing to Cyber Hubs, CSIRTs (computer security incident response teams) and competent authorities under favourable market conditions.
cards.sources: Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 11–14 · CYBERAI, Scope

cards.title: Problem
cards.question: What type of problem or need must justify the project, and where must it originate?
cards.answer:
The need is that of national cybersecurity authorities and the operators they protect, who must analyse growing volumes of threat data faster.
The call names Cyber Hubs, CSIRTs, competent authorities, public bodies and private entities covered by the NIS 2 Directive (the EU law that sets cybersecurity duties for essential and important entities, including electricity operators) as the users. These bodies hold the input data for AI-based tools and protect providers of critical infrastructure and essential services. A second need is the security of AI systems themselves, including misuse of AI by attackers.
cards.sources: Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 11–14 · CYBERAI, Objectives; Scope

cards.title: Deliverables
cards.question: Which concrete outputs must the project produce?
cards.answer:
Deployed AI-based cybersecurity tools, services or infrastructures, plus mandatory reporting deliverables.
- Novel AI-based tools developed, tested and validated in relevant conditions and made available to Cyber Hubs, CSIRTs and similar bodies
- Tools that automate creating, analysing and processing CTI; original European CTI feeds or services
- Secure, legally compliant AI solutions for NIS sectors
- A dissemination and exploitation deliverable within the first six months
- Yearly deliverables named Project Outputs and KPIs (key performance indicators) M12, M24 and so on, classified as sensitive

cards.title: Impact
cards.question: Which wider system outcomes and impacts must the project support?
cards.answer:
The project must strengthen the ability of Cyber Hubs, CSIRTs and NIS 2 entities to detect and handle threats, and report this through set indicators.
Mandatory topic indicators:
- Number of entities benefiting from the AI-powered cybersecurity technologies, tools and services
- Number of AI-powered capabilities provided to Cyber Hubs and national authorities
Optional topic indicators include tools for automated threat detection and incident response, and the number of cybersecure tools that reduce risk where AI, IoT and smart grids meet. All projects also report the programme's common indicators: infrastructures, tools and services deployed; users with access; entities supported in preparing for major incidents; and dissemination activities. The call sets no numerical targets: applicants propose their own baselines and targets.
cards.sources:
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 11–14 · CYBERAI, Expected Outcome; KPIs

cards.title: After the project
cards.question: How must the result be replicated, taken up and kept in use after the project?
cards.answer:
The results must be designed for wider use: they must be licensable to Cyber Hubs, CSIRTs and authorities across the EU.
- Transferability: the systems, tools and services will be made available for licensing to National and Cross-Border Cyber Hubs, CSIRTs and competent authorities under favourable market conditions.
- Standards: projects should contribute to standardisation and certification of cybersecure, trustworthy AI.
- Exploitation limits: results must be exploited in EU or EEA countries, and transfers and licensing of results are restricted for security reasons.
- Dissemination: a communication and dissemination plan and a dissemination deliverable are mandatory. The call does not say who must operate the tools after the grant ends.
cards.sources:

cards.title: Number of partners
cards.question: What is the permitted or required consortium size?
cards.answer: No minimum: a single organisation may apply, although consortia are encouraged.
cards.sources: Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · p. 50 · 6. Consortium composition

cards.title: Partner composition
cards.question: Which types of partners must the consortium include?
cards.answer:
The call requires no partner types; it targets a broad mix of organisations.
Targeted stakeholders are technology providers, operators of Cyber Hubs, research and academia, cybersecurity entities, the public sector, NIS 2 entities and the private sector. Links with high-performance computing stakeholders should be made where appropriate. Every participant must be established in and controlled from an EU or EEA country.
cards.sources:
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 11–14 · CYBERAI, Scope; Targeted stakeholders
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · p. 48 · 6. Eligibility

cards.title: Distribution of work
cards.question: How must work and budget be distributed among partners?
cards.answer:
The call sets no split of work or budget; main participants should be beneficiaries, and subcontracting should stay limited.
Organisations doing a substantial share of the work should join as beneficiaries or affiliated entities (linked entities that receive part of the grant). Associated partners and providers of in-kind contributions take part at their own cost. Subcontracting beyond 30% of eligible costs is only possible in very exceptional cases.
cards.sources: Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · p. 65 · 13. Important, Consortium roles

cards.title: Coordinator
cards.question: What type of organisation may or must act as lead applicant?
cards.answer:
Any eligible legal entity may coordinate; the call does not restrict the role.
In a consortium the beneficiaries choose a coordinator, who manages the project, represents the consortium and receives all payments. A single applicant is automatically coordinator.
cards.sources:
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · p. 65 · 13. Important, Coordinator
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · p. 60 · 10. Reporting and payment arrangements

project_requirements.title: TenneT's position
project_requirements.question: What is TenneT's position within the consortium?

cards.title: Coordinate
cards.question: Can TenneT apply or coordinate, and under which conditions?
cards.answer:
Yes: TenneT TSO B.V. could apply alone or coordinate a consortium.
Any public or private legal entity may be a beneficiary (a partner that receives part of the grant) if it is established in an EU Member State, Norway, Iceland or Liechtenstein and is not directly or indirectly controlled from any other country.
This security restriction (Article 12(5) of the Digital Europe Regulation, the EU law that sets up the programme) applies to every topic of this call and to every role: beneficiary, affiliated entity, associated partner and subcontractor. Every participant must submit an ownership control declaration, except entities validated as public bodies. All project work, including subcontracted work, must take place in those eligible countries. TenneT TSO B.V. is a Dutch company owned by the Dutch State, so it meets these conditions; it must still file the declaration if it is not validated as a public body. In practice a coordinator here would develop or deploy AI cybersecurity tools; TenneT would more plausibly join a provider-led consortium than lead one.
cards.sources:
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 48–50 · 6. Eligibility
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 69–70 · Annex 2

cards.title: Participate
cards.question: Can TenneT take part without receiving funding?
cards.answer:
Yes, either as a funded beneficiary or as an associated partner at its own cost.
An associated partner takes part in the work without receiving grant money and need not be validated, but must still meet the EU-control restriction and file an ownership control declaration. TenneT could use this role, for example to provide a test environment or operational feedback, if it does not want to manage grant obligations.
cards.sources:
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · p. 65 · 13. Important, Associated partners
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · p. 48 · 6. Eligibility

cards.title: Receive funding
cards.question: Can TenneT receive funding, and which funding rate or cost rules apply?
cards.answer:
Yes, at 50% of its eligible costs as a beneficiary.
The 50% rate is the same for all organisations in this topic. TenneT would have to fund the other half itself. Costs only count for work done in EU or EEA countries, indirect costs are a flat 7% of direct costs, and the grant may not produce a profit. The call has no separate Dutch funding rules: the ECCC (European Cybersecurity Competence Centre, the EU body that manages the call) funds all partners directly.
cards.sources:
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · p. 13–14 · CYBERAI, Type of action and funding rate
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 57–59 · 10. Form of grant; Budget categories and cost eligibility rules

cards.title: TenneT's likely contribution
cards.question: What contribution would make TenneT credible and useful within the project?
cards.answer:
TenneT would be most credible as the critical-infrastructure operator that supplies the operational setting for AI-based threat detection in control systems.
The scope explicitly names anomaly detection in Operational Technology and risk reduction where AI, IoT and smart grids meet. TenneT could provide OT security requirements, anonymised network or event data, a test environment (for example via its digital twin facilities) and validation of tools by its security operations team. It could also link the project to the Dutch national cyber authorities and CSIRT that the tools are meant to serve. This is an interpretation: the call does not name TSOs.
cards.sources: Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 11–14 · CYBERAI, Scope; Targeted stakeholders

project_requirements.title: Innovation
project_requirements.question: What type of innovation must the project develop?

cards.title: Innovation threshold
cards.question: Must the project produce genuinely new knowledge or technology, or may it integrate and apply existing solutions?
cards.answer:
The project should develop and deploy new AI-based tools, but may build on existing ones; the call asks for novel tools validated in relevant conditions.
The scope asks to develop and deploy systems and tools; the expected outcomes speak of novel cybersecurity tools based on AI that have been developed, tested and validated. Proposals are scored on the maturity of the project, so ready-to-deploy work is favoured.
cards.sources:
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 11–14 · CYBERAI, Scope; Expected Outcome
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · p. 55 · 9. Award criteria

cards.title: Innovation object
cards.question: In what must the project innovate?
cards.answer:
Mainly technology: AI-based detection, response and threat-intelligence tools, plus security of AI systems.
The call also includes operational methods (automation of cybersecurity processes in Cyber Hubs, information sharing between authorities) and contributions to standardisation and certification.
cards.sources: Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 11–14 · CYBERAI, Scope; Expected Outcome

cards.title: Development stages
cards.question: Which development stages must the project cover?
cards.answer:
Development, testing, validation and deployment: the call is a deployment programme, not a research call.
Tools must be developed, tested and validated in relevant conditions and made available to users; research activities alone do not fit.
cards.sources:
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 11–14 · CYBERAI, Scope; Expected Outcome
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · p. 4 · 0. Introduction

cards.title: Maturity
cards.question: Which maturity level is expected at the start and end of the project?
cards.answer: The call sets no TRL (technology readiness level). It asks for tools validated in relevant conditions and scores the maturity of the project.
cards.sources:
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 11–14 · CYBERAI, Expected Outcome
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · p. 55 · 9. Award criteria

project_requirements.title: Work
project_requirements.question: Which activities or work structure must the project cover?

cards.title: Demonstration
cards.question: Where and under which conditions must the solution be demonstrated?
cards.answer:
Tools must be tested and validated in relevant conditions and deployed for real users; the call does not prescribe a laboratory or live setting.
The call asks for deployment to Cyber Hubs, CSIRTs, national authorities and NIS sectors, and counts CTI feeds deployed in an operational environment as an optional indicator.
cards.sources: Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 11–14 · CYBERAI, Expected Outcome; KPIs

cards.title: Integration
cards.question: How must the activities fit together and with existing systems?
cards.answer:
The call does not demand one integrated system, but tools must fit into the operations of Cyber Hubs and authorities.
The tools should automate Cyber Hub processes and support information sharing between Cyber Hubs, CSIRTs and other bodies; links with high-performance computing are encouraged and EuroHPC (the EU supercomputer network) access may be granted in justified cases.
cards.sources: Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 11–14 · CYBERAI, Scope; Expected Outcome

cards.title: Evidence
cards.question: What must the demonstration prove?
cards.answer:
Evidence comes from the indicators the applicant proposes, reported yearly with baselines, targets and means of verification.
Mandatory indicators count the entities benefiting and the AI capabilities provided to Cyber Hubs and authorities. Each indicator must be measurable and verifiable, set out in the call's KPI table (identifier, baseline, target, unit, method, data source, responsible entity, verification).
cards.sources:
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 11–14 · CYBERAI, KPIs
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 9–11 · 2. Guidance on milestones, deliverables and KPIs

cards.title: User participation
cards.question: How must users take part in the project?
cards.answer:
The call names the users (Cyber Hubs, CSIRTs, authorities, NIS 2 entities) but does not require them to co-design or test the tools.
Tool providers may apply in consortium with Cyber Hubs, and the expected outcome is tools made available to these users.
cards.sources: Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 11–14 · CYBERAI, Scope; Targeted stakeholders

cards.title: Safety and cybersecurity
cards.question: Which safety, cybersecurity or data requirements must the project meet?
cards.answer:
Strict security rules apply: only EU- or EEA-controlled entities, work only in eligible countries, and Cyber Hubs must be protected against foreign dependencies.
- The AI solutions must themselves be cybersecure, robust and trustworthy, and comply with the AI Act, intellectual property law and the GDPR.
- Proposals involving AI undergo an ethics review of human oversight, fairness, transparency and social impact; experts also assess robustness.
- Projects handling EU classified information need security scrutiny, and grant signature requires at least one beneficiary with facility security clearance.
- Results may only be exploited in eligible countries, with limits on transfers and licensing.

funding_timing_submission.title: Funding
funding_timing_submission.question: How much funding can the project receive?

cards.title: Funding envelope
cards.answer:
About EUR 3–5 million of EU funding per project, from a topic budget of EUR 15 million for about 4 projects.
- Total project size: the call states no project size; at the 50% rate a EUR 3–5 million grant implies total eligible costs of about EUR 6–10 million.
- Grant request: per project; other amounts may be requested if duly justified, and the grant awarded may be lower than requested.
- Funding form: budget-based mixed actual-cost grant (actual costs incurred are reimbursed, with some unit-cost and flat-rate elements, not the budgeted amounts).
cards.sources:
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · p. 46 · 3. Available budget
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · p. 57 · 10. Form of grant, funding rate and maximum grant amount
Topic page, Budget overview (EU Funding & Tenders Portal)

cards.title: Funding rate and co-financing
cards.answer:
A single rate of 50% of eligible costs applies to every partner, whatever its size.
- Co-financing conditions: the other 50% must come from the partners' own resources or other income; Simple Grants (the call's standard grant type) pay no higher rate for SMEs in this topic.
- Evidence required: no co-financing letter is required; the financial capacity check during grant preparation looks at whether each beneficiary can carry its share.
cards.sources:

cards.title: Budget constraints
cards.answer:
Only actual costs of work in eligible countries count, with a 7% flat rate for indirect costs.
- Eligible costs: personnel (average personnel costs allowed), subcontracting, travel (actual costs only), equipment, other goods and services, internally invoiced goods and services, indirect costs.
- Caps or mandatory allocations: subcontracting should normally be a limited part; going beyond 30% of total eligible costs is only possible in very exceptional cases and must be justified.
- Excluded costs: costs of activities outside the EU and EEA countries; separate project websites; in-kind contributions given for free cannot be declared as costs.
- Overheads and VAT: indirect costs at a flat 7% of eligible direct costs; non-deductible VAT is eligible, except VAT paid by public bodies acting as public authority.
- Subcontracting or equipment: for this topic the full cost of listed equipment may be charged, besides depreciation of other equipment; subcontracted work must be performed in eligible countries.
cards.sources:
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 58–59 · 10. Budget categories and cost eligibility rules
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · p. 65 · 13. Important, Consortium roles

cards.title: Cash flow and financial exposure
cards.answer:
Most of the grant is paid up front, but grants may not make a profit and overpayments are recovered.
- Payment model: prefinancing of normally 80% of the maximum grant after signature, one or more interim payments, then the balance; all payments go to the coordinator.
- Retention or guarantee: a prefinancing guarantee, normally from the coordinator, may be required if financial capacity is judged weak; public bodies are not checked for financial capacity.
- Financial reporting or audit: for-profit organisations must declare revenues and any profit is deducted from the final grant.

funding_timing_submission.title: Timing
funding_timing_submission.question: What timing should the proposal submission and project follow?

cards.title: Application route
cards.answer:
One stage: a full proposal submitted online through the EU Funding & Tenders Portal by 14 January 2027, 17:00 CET (Brussels).
- Stage 1 — Full proposal: 14 January 2027, 17:00:00 CET; Part A (administrative data and budget, filled in online), Part B (technical description, at most 70 pages) and ownership control declarations for all participants; every beneficiary, affiliated entity and associated partner needs a PIC (a 9-digit participant identification code from the Participant Register).
- Additional procedure: none; each proposal may address only one topic of the call.

cards.title: Project window
cards.answer:
An indicative duration of 36 months, starting after grant signature, which is expected in October 2027.
- Maximum duration: 36 months indicative; other durations are not excluded and extensions are possible through an amendment if duly justified.
- Required start: normally after grant signature; a retroactive start may exceptionally be granted, but never before the proposal submission date.
- Eligible-cost period: from the start date fixed in the grant agreement.

cards.title: Decision and contracting
cards.answer:
Results are expected in April 2027 and grant signature in October 2027 (both indicative).
- Expected invitation or assessment result: evaluation February–March 2027; information on results April 2027.
- Funding decision: April 2027, indicative; an invitation to grant preparation is not yet a commitment to fund.
- Grant agreement: October 2027, indicative.
- Conditions before starting: legal entity validation, financial capacity and exclusion checks, ownership control assessment, ethics review; a consortium agreement where there is more than one beneficiary; if EU classified information is involved, at least one beneficiary must hold facility security clearance before signature.

funding_timing_submission.title: Application
funding_timing_submission.question: Mandatory information to include in the application

cards.title: Mandatory submission package — pass/fail
cards.answer:
The proposal must contain Part A, Part B and ownership control declarations, all through the Portal submission system.
- Application form: Part A online; Part B downloaded from the submission system, at most 70 pages; any official EU language, but the abstract must be in English and English is strongly advised.
- Budget: summarised budget in Part A; no detailed budget table is required.
- Mandatory annexes: ownership control declarations, including for associated partners and subcontractors.
- Partner documents: the coordinator confirms a mandate to act for all applicants; each beneficiary signs a declaration of honour before grant signature.
- Registration: EU Login account and PIC for every participant; beneficiaries are validated by the Central Validation Service.
cards.sources:
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 47–48 · 5. Admissibility and documents
Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 62, 64–65 · 11. How to submit; 13. Important, Registration; Language

cards.title: Evaluation and selection — scored or ranked
cards.answer:
Proposals are scored on relevance, implementation and impact, each out of 5, and need at least 3 on each and 10 overall.
- Evaluation criteria: relevance (fit with the topic, policy contribution, supply-chain security where applicable); implementation (maturity, soundness of the plan, capacity of the applicants); impact (expected outcomes, competitiveness and benefits for society).
- Thresholds: 3 out of 5 per criterion; 10 out of 15 overall.
- Ranking rules: ties are broken first by themes not covered by higher-ranked proposals, then by the relevance score, then by the impact score, then by portfolio considerations.
- Budget assessment: the grant awarded may be lower than requested and costs may be adjusted in grant preparation.
cards.sources: Call Document  DEP 11.pdf · pp. 54–56 · 8. Evaluation and award procedure; 9. Award criteria

cards.title: Conditional and exceptional requirements
cards.answer:
A few conditions depend on the project's content.
- Conditional — EU classified information: security scrutiny and a security aspects letter; at least one beneficiary must have facility security clearance before signature, or the grant cannot be signed.
- Conditional — AI systems: ethics review of AI-specific principles; ethics deliverables may be added to the grant.
- Exception — award criteria: for this topic, overcoming lack of market finance and environmental sustainability are not scored.
- Recommended: apply for membership of the Cybersecurity Competence Community (the ECCC's network of cybersecurity organisations) through the National Coordination Centre and attach proof.
